item.title: 4 Samsung apps I thought were bloatware until I actually started using them
item.itunes:title: 4 Samsung apps I thought were bloatware until I actually started using them
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I'm always somewhat wary of pre-installed apps on my smartphones, even when it comes to my Samsung Galaxy devices. However, over the years, I've realized that some apps I initially thought were bloatware turned out to actually be useful. In some cases, the apps were so good that I actually preferred them to third-party alternatives.

From productivity boosters to more creative applications, I was surprised by how much these pre-installed Samsung apps actually ended up impressing me.

4 apps I always remove from every Samsung Galaxy phone

Samsung's own apps, although decent, aren't all worth keeping.

14
By  Hamlin Rozario

Samsung Notes

More than meets the eye

Samsung's Notes app seems unassuming at first. It's a simple sticky-note-style app that lets you take notes with your phone's keyboard or an S-Pen if you have a compatible device.

However, once you search a little bit beneath the surface, you start to realize just how much it can do. You can upload PDFs to the app, which you can then annotate or fill in using text or drawings. In fact, you can use the app to scan and edit documents that you need to keep on hand.

For handwritten notes, you can use AI to convert them into text. These AI features also extend to other notes and documents, allowing you to summarize and translate them. You can also attach voice recordings, images, drawings, and tables.

In terms of organization, you can use folders to sort your notes. This adds a bit of order to your scattered notes. When creating new notes, you can choose different styles, including lined pages and planners. While it seems simple at first, Samsung Notes is more versatile than I expected.

Samsung Reminder

My favorite Samsung app

The Reminder app is one of those Samsung apps I wish I'd discovered years ago. One of its most powerful features is how it puts different reminder types front and center, including location- and schedule-based reminders. It also provides a series of suggested templates you can try out.

This makes it one of the most user-friendly task and reminder apps I've ever encountered. As much as I love my main to-do list app TickTick, I wish it took more inspiration from Samsung Reminder's design. Currently, I run a series of scheduled reminders in the app, including a monthly reminder to take my migraine medication out of the fridge. I also set up the app on my boyfriend's phone to remind him to take his insulin out of the fridge before he leaves work.

If you haven't tried the app and you own a Galaxy device, I can't recommend it enough. It makes setting reminders and tasks intuitive rather than another chore.

PENUP

A creative outlet

The PENUP app was something I tried out of curiosity rather than any immediate need. However, the mobile drawing app became one I genuinely loved using. You can use it on a phone without a stylus, but it works best on phones with an S-Pen.

The app lets you create drawings from scratch, trace over an existing image, and color in pages created by others. Even if you're not an artist, it makes for a great creative outlet.

You can also share your creations with others or browse the images others have posted. However, I enjoy using it most to practice drawing and creating images I don't share.

Samsung Browser

A well-rounded alternative to Chrome

While I use Brave as my preferred browser, Samsung Browser is a great alternative if you have a smartphone from the Korean giant. If you enjoy AI features, you'll be glad to know the browser includes a range of AI capabilities, including summarizing and translating pages, as well as reading highlights aloud. It also lets you choose your preferred ad blocker for the browser app.

One of my favorite features is the ability to force dark mode on web pages without using a flag. You can even adjust how bright you want pages to be in dark mode. Like Firefox, the app lets you install extensions to further customize your experience, which is helpful for power users.

Like many other Samsung apps, it also has user-friendliness in its favor. You can adjust the text size on sites on the fly without navigating buried accessibility menus. You can also customize your toolbar so that your most important shortcuts are at the forefront. For example, you can save a button to turn off ad blocking temporarily.

Samsung Browser has become so popular that Samsung has even brought the app to Windows PCs. This cross-platform availability, including syncing, is another reason to use the browser over third-party alternatives.

I turned my Samsung Galaxy into a speed machine by ditching Samsung's bloated launcher

The official launcher is of no good.

1
By  Anurag Singh

Samsung's pre-installed apps are some of my favorites

While I definitely uninstall some Samsung apps, the company makes some of my favorite first-party apps of any brand. Many times, if I don't use one of these apps, it's simply because I switch phone brands every few years and prefer to keep cross-platform solutions like Notesnook in my rotation.

But if you're deeply invested in the Samsung ecosystem and haven't tried these apps, I recommend checking them out. They may offer far more value than you expect.

item.title: I gave Windows 11’s Start menu a complete overhaul with one open-source app
item.itunes:title: I gave Windows 11’s Start menu a complete overhaul with one open-source app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When it comes to the Windows 11 Start menu, users either love its layout and design or hate that it takes up most of the screen when opened. On top of that, Windows' native search feature is slow and clunky. Luckily, third-party utilities like Everything or File Pilot can improve the experience with better search.

Another app lets you overhaul the Start menu and provides a better search experience. Flow Launcher is something you can try if you are fed up with the default Start menu and want to find what you need faster.

Get Flow Launcher onboard

Replacing the Start menu with a better experience

Flow Launcher is an app launcher and file and folder search utility that I use to virtually replace the Start menu on Windows 11. It's also available for those still running Windows 10 and can be installed like a normal app, or you can use the portable version and run it from a USB Flash drive. It's not only an app launcher; it can also find files and folders more easily than Windows' native search.

Windows search is extremely slow and clunky, and it often serves up Bing results instead of the item you're looking for. It relies on a sluggish underlying indexing service that's supposed to mimic Spotlight on macOS, but it does it horribly. I can usually find a file or folder faster by poking around in File Explorer myself by the time the search is half finished — with incorrect results, by the way.

Opening Flow Launcher is easy enough with Alt + Space. It also includes keyboard shortcuts for the app's features; they appear while you are installing Flow Launcher. For instance, you can go back to the Context menu with Esc or press Ctrl + Enter to open containing folders. It finds files, folders, and launches apps far faster than Windows Search. Otherwise, it stays hidden unless you want it to show. I like to leave it hidden, so I have more room to work on what I need. Type in what you're looking for and open it — it's that simple.

Flow Launcher

Flow Launcher is a simple, yet incredibly versatile search bar for Windows that can launch apps, files, and more.

See at Flow Launcher

Using Flow Launcher

It's straightforward and finds what you need fast

Once I got the hang of Flow Launcher, I stopped hitting the Windows key to open the Start menu unless it was muscle memory, because I found a better way to find the apps and files I need. Flow Launcher brings the items right to me; there is no reason to hit the Windows key and search for items anymore. Then I discovered the plugins available for it, and one in particular that is quite powerful for search.

I also own a Mac, so I am familiar with how Spotlight works, and this is the closest alternative I've found for Windows. It is a minimalist floating box on my desktop that brings up exactly what I'm looking for, along with matching files and settings I might want to access. For instance, if I type in Jellyfin, it brings up the server, tray apps, executables I may want to run, recent searches, and more.

I like it because it uses Action Keywords, a more natural language than coding-style prefixes. I can type short prefixes that tell Flow Launcher which tool or plugin should handle my query. I can type a keyword, space, and my query to get the results I want. I don't need to type in code to find and manage data. However, I do need to know a few symbols, like > to run a Command Prompt query or b to search web browser bookmarks, or s for Windows settings. The point is, it's not too complicated to learn the utility, get things done, and work faster in Windows from the keyboard while ignoring the Start menu.

10 best Flow Launcher plug-ins to get things done faster

Speed up your workflow using your keyboard

By  João Carrasqueira

Find Everything

Search Everything with Flow Launcher

Flow Launcher does a great job of finding apps, files, and folders on your local drive. However, you can connect the Everything app to really add search power to Flow Launcher. Once connected, you can search for items across all drives connected to your PC. After I connected Everything to Flow Launcher and tweaked a few settings, I could search other drives for apps, movies, shows, music files, and other items. Once I added it, I could search for items across all my drives, like with Everything, but with a unified, keyboard-first interface.

It adds the same indexing and search capabilities of Everything to the launcher — making Flow Launcher a more powerful search tool by pressing Alt + Space to summon the interface. You can still use Everything as a standalone app to search for, well, everything on all your drives. Connecting it to Flow Launcher lets me press the dedicated keyboard combination to decide what I may need next, like an app, a Windows Setting, a command, a bookmark, or another item.

5 Start menu alternatives and Windows tweaks that will speed up your workflow

Revamp your Windows experience with smarter Start menu alternatives and tweaks—boost efficiency, streamline navigation, and work faster

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Plugin Enhancement

An entire store of helpful plugin tools

Another incredible addition to this open-source app is the number of available plugins. Press Alt + Space to launch Flow Launcher, type settings, and choose Tweak Flow Launcher's Settings. Open the Plugins tab on the left, and you'll find numerous plugins ready to use out of the box. For example, the File Explorer plugin is where you add Everything. Other plugins can make your work easier, like searching through bookmarks, improving the Calculator app's calculation abilities, and more.

There is also a plugin store with even more options to help with your workflow or play. Plugins vary depending on the type of workflow you are looking for. You can use basic ones like the weather plugin to check weather conditions with your keyboard, or more productivity-focused plugins for coders and developers, or to keep track of your work in Obsidian. But there is also room for fun. For instance, the Spotify plugin lets you control music and podcast playback with keyboard strokes.

7 app launchers that will speed up your productivity on Windows

Launch apps with the press of a key

3
By  Sumukh Rao

Flow Launcher beats the Start menu by leaps and bounds

The Start menu is nothing compared to Flow Launcher's power. Connecting it to the Everything utility makes it more powerful than the Start menu, which just shows apps and lets you click them. Flow Launcher is powerful, stays out of your way, and only appears when you need it. It's a compact tool that every Windows user should have. PowerToys Run comes close, but Flow Launcher is even better and offers more functionality for serious work or when you want to take a break and play. Once I started using it, I've virtually forgotten about the Start menu and have no desire to use it.

item.title: Home Assistant blueprints finally stopped my copy-paste automation nightmare
item.itunes:title: Home Assistant blueprints finally stopped my copy-paste automation nightmare
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When building your own automations, it's so easy to fall victim to the copy-paste trap. If you write a brilliant motion-activated lighting automation for your hallway, it works perfectly, and then you go out and buy sensors for your kitchen, bathroom, and basement too.

When you're copy-pasting the same raw YAML block four times and manually swapping out the entity IDs, you're actually creating a sprawling disorganized list of near-identical automations. Realistically, the best course of action is to dive into Home Assistant blueprints, which are reusable automation templates that separate the structural logic from the physical device entities.

Smart home configuration shouldn't feel like repetitive manual labor. By embracing Home Assistant blueprints and community-driven templates, you can turn messy duplicate scripts into clean centralized functions, slashing your maintenance overhead and keeping your home lab organized.

I replaced my smart bulbs with smart relays and saved my family from home automation fatigue

Your smart home shouldn't cause friction.

42
By  Jasmine Mannan

What are Home Assistant blueprints?

You can make automation so much easier

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

For those who aren't familiar with Home Assistant blueprints, the architecture behind them works essentially like a function within code. Every individual automation you spin up from it is a function call. The blueprint defines the core shape of the automation, like the triggers, the condition logic, and action sequences, but then it leaves the placeholder variables open for physical devices. When you want to apply a Home Assistant blueprint to a new room, you fill out a clean visual form instead of writing YAML or copying and pasting old automations and replacing entity IDs.

You get the benefit of global inheritance and updates because they instantly inherit their behavior from the parent blueprint. This means updating the master template instantly propagates performance tweaks or bug fixes across every room using it (instead of you having to go through each individual automation you've typed out and repair it).

The benefits of adopting blueprints

There are countless real-world applications

Swapping over to blueprints feels like the obvious choice once you really understand how it can save your sanity with these real-world wins. Swapping over to blueprints completely changes how you manage your home. You get standardized motion and presence lighting. Managing a dozen rooms with motion sensors, ambient light level checks, and time-of-day offsets using a single master blueprint (instead of maintaining twelve individual spaghetti automations) makes any adjustments you need to make throughout the year super simple.

You also get low-battery and health-monitoring dashboards because you can deploy a global battery-level monitoring blueprint that scans every Zigbee and Z-Wave device on your network. It can automatically cue notifications when a coin cell drops below 15%, so you never have to worry about checking the battery levels on all of your devices individually.

You can also leverage the community blueprint exchange. With so many users actively using Home Assistant, there's a large, prebuilt, heavily tested community template database for complex tasks. If you're looking to automate something, chances are someone's already done it and uploaded the blueprint for you. Right down to Frigate AI camera notification routing, climate schedules, and even smart switch scene controllers. You can take advantage of all of this without having to reinvent the wheel or do any YAML coding yourself.

Blueprints won't always be perfect

But here's how to get started with them for the times they do work

Credit: Break a Layer

It's worth noting that sometimes blueprints do fall short. They're not always going to be the right fit because, ultimately, your home is only your home. If you have any hope of a specific automation that relies on complex branching conditional logic that is entirely unique to a single device and will likely never be reused anywhere else in the house, a standard custom automation or Node-RED flow is often cleaner than having to pick up a blueprint and adjust it for that specific purpose.

Sometimes when you're adopting a blueprint, it can be overwhelming to the point that you fall into a massive multipage form with 40 different toggle inputs. That essentially defeats the purpose of the simplicity that blueprints bring you. If a blueprint becomes too complicated, it loses its elegance, so don't over-parameterize it.

If you're hoping to get started with Home Assistant blueprints, then the best first step is to audit your duplicate automations by looking through your Home Assistant dashboard for automations that share identical logic but target different rooms or devices. Then extract the core logic. Take your most robust working automation, strip out the hard-coded entity IDs and replace them with `!input` declarations; then you can define the selectors like `entity`, `device`, or `area` so that the UI provides clean drop-down menus when you implement these blueprints. Lastly, clean up all of your automations by importing your new custom blueprint. Spin up instances for each room and safely delete the legacy duplicates you've got going on.

Don't let YAML drag you down

Blueprints can save you so much time

Home automation should simplify your life, not saddle you with what feels like a second part-time job maintaining bloated code. Shifting from brute-force copying to modular blueprints transforms Home Assistant from a cluttered hobby project into a resilient enterprise-grade local platform. Copying and pasting raw YAML files can be messy and frustrating, and blueprints essentially remove that friction.

item.title: You are using Android Auto wrong if you haven't tried these features
item.itunes:title: You are using Android Auto wrong if you haven't tried these features
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Android Auto is one of those tools that can feel complete the moment you plug in your phone. You get Google Maps, music, calls, messages, and that is usually enough to get through a daily commute. That is how I used it for a long time, too.

But after digging through its settings and paying more attention to the smaller features Google has added over time, I realized I was barely scratching the surface.

4 key Android Auto features I rely on to stay safe while driving

Gemini voice commands, Waze navigation, organizing Android Auto's launcher, and more are key to keeping me locked in on the road.

3
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Use Gemini for more than navigation

Make sure to give it access to your favorite apps first

I used to treat Gemini in Android Auto as little more than a hands-free shortcut for Google Maps. I would ask it to navigate somewhere, check the weather, or call a contact. Gemini becomes far more useful once you connect it to the apps you already use on your phone.

I went through Gemini settings on my phone, found the Connected Apps menu, and connected it to my preferred services, including Google Workspace, WhatsApp, YouTube Music, and Messages.

That changed how I use voice commands while driving. I can say something like, ‘Add pick up groceries to my Tasks,’ and Gemini does the job in no time. I can even ask Gemini to create a specific note just via a voice command in my car.

Messaging is another big one for me. I can ask, ‘Message Rachel saying I will be home in 20 minutes and ask if she wants me to grab anything from the route?’ Gemini supports sending WhatsApp messages and regular text pings.

I can also ask it to play a specific artist, playlist, or define a movie scene, and Gemini understands my request and brings up the song in no time. For instance, when I asked it to play that rooftop song in the Suits series, it understood that I was talking about the ‘Whatever it takes’ song and played the same.

These may sound like small conveniences individually, but together they make Gemini a powerful copilot (not the Microsoft one) for your long, tiring trips.

Change how message notifications behave

Turn off distractions

Message notifications were one of those small Android Auto annoyances I ignored for too long. Every incoming message would make a chime, and Android Auto would also show the first line of the message on the screen. They are not distracting, but when I am driving through traffic, even that small interruption is enough to pull my attention away for a second.

I eventually went through Android Auto settings and disabled Play message chime and Show first line of messages toggles. The difference was immediate. Messages can still arrive, but my dashboard feels much quieter and less demanding now.

I no longer hear a notification sound every time someone texts me, and I am tempted to glance at a message preview just because a few words suddenly appear on the screen.

I still have access to my messages when I actually need them. If something looks important, I can use Gemini to read aloud or reply using my voice. That gives me the best of both worlds.

The Android Auto feature nobody talks about but everyone should use

Stop ignoring this hidden Android Auto gem.

By  Parth Shah

Try Waze instead of blindly sticking with Maps

Explore offline music players, too

Google Maps is the obvious default on Android Auto, and I used it almost automatically for a long time. But once I started trying other apps, I realized the default option isn't always the best for every drive.

Waze, for example, works better for me on shorter city routes because the interface feels cleaner and its real-time reports for traffic, hazards, and road conditions are easier to notice at a glance. I still prefer Google Maps for longer trips and offline navigation, but I no longer use it for everything.

I took the same approach with music. Instead of always relying on a streaming app like YouTube Music, I tried Poweramp with my local music library. It turned out to be a much better option when I want to tweak the audio output or prefer a solid experience in offline areas.

Android Auto becomes much more useful once I stop treating Google’s default apps as the only options.

Explore Gemini Actions

And pin them on the dashboard

One Android Auto feature I started using a lot is Gemini Actions. Instead of repeating the same voice command every time I get into the car, I can create an action for something I do frequently and pin it directly to the Android Auto dashboard.

I have a few of these set up around my normal driving routine. One action sends my ETA to my wife, another starts playing downloaded music, and another finds nearby restaurants.

Check out my dedicated post to learn more about Gemini actions in Android Auto.

Use Android Auto beyond the basics

Android Auto works perfectly fine with its default setup, but that does not mean you should leave it that way. Once I started making these changes, the whole experience became much better suited to how I actually drive. If you use Android Auto regularly, it is worth spending a few minutes exploring beyond Maps and music.

item.title: COSMIC 1.9 finally gets its own image viewer, and it even comes with its own editing tools
item.itunes:title: COSMIC 1.9 finally gets its own image viewer, and it even comes with its own editing tools
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • COSMIC Viewer debuts in Epoch 1.9.0 as a native image viewer.
  • Offers EXIF-aware details, non-destructive edits, annotations, and a hex color picker.
  • Also adds COSMIC OSK virtual keyboard, Store UI refresh, and many bug fixes.

The COSMIC desktop environment hasn't even celebrated its first anniversary of its public release, after it officially entered the scene in December 2025. However, it's already making big waves within the community, with several Linux distros supporting it outside of its home at Pop!_OS. Now, COSMIC fans will be pleased to hear that the desktop environment has its own image viewer, and it does more than just show you your family photos.

COSMIC Epoch 1.9.0 introduces COSMIC Viewer into the mix

It seems like a solid image viewer despite being brand new

Credit: System76

Over on the COSMIC GitHub repo, the System76 team has announced the release of Epoch 1.9.0. My favorite feature from the list is COSMIC Viewer, which finally gives the desktop environment its own unique tool for viewing images without relying on external tools.

It comes with all the basics you'd expect from an image viewer, including navigation, zoom, and saving the image. However, it also comes with some very nice tools that some years-old operating systems still haven't managed:

  • EXIF-aware image details
  • Non-destructive editing: crop, rotate, undo/redo, and revert all
  • Annotation: freehand pen, highlighter, shapes (rectangle, ellipse, arrow, line, star, polygon), and text
  • Custom colors via a hex/RGB picker with recent colors
  • Clipboard: copy the image or its file path
  • Set as wallpaper on the current or all displays
  • Move to trash from within the viewer

If you're not interested in image viewers, COSMIC Epoch 1.9.0 also adds COSMIC OSK, a virtual keyboard that accepts touch and gamepad inputs. The COSMIC Store got a new coat of paint, which mainly focuses on better showing who developed each app. Plus, there's a ton of bug fixes for all the apps you know and love already.

I switched to the COSMIC Linux desktop, and I can't wait for the future

COSMIC is out of this world, even with its flaws

item.title: I felt my GPU connector get dangerously warm, so I bought a $140 babysitter for my power cables
item.itunes:title: I felt my GPU connector get dangerously warm, so I bought a $140 babysitter for my power cables
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Recently, I pulled my RTX 5080 out of my system while doing some maintenance, and, quite concerningly, the 12V-2x6 connector that was plugged into the front of my card was quite warm. Not the usual warmth that emits from your system after a long gaming session, but a warmth that seemed...off.

I recalled that Steve from Hardware Unboxed recently experienced something similar, and ended up experiencing a failure on his RTX 5090, and that was enough for me to shop around for some kind of protection. I settled on the WireView Pro II from Thermal Grizzly, and while the 5080 doesn't push even close to the same wattage as the 5090, cards have experienced catastrophic melting failures at and around the TDP of the 5080. This tool doesn't fix the connector itself, but it can shut things down before any damage happens, and that's good enough for me.

Someone's RTX 5090's power connector reached 300°F during a test

Don't touch this.

By  Simon Batt

What the WireView Pro II actually measures

It's a really neat piece of tech

The WireView Pro II is essentially a power adapter for your GPU that includes a screen, an integrated fan, and some optional temperature probes. It plugs into the card's 12V-2x6 socket, your cable plugs into it, and it measures current on each individual pin along with voltage, temperature, and total power. On my MSI RTX 5080 Shadow 3X OC, it sits over the card's connector and sends the cable straight down, so there's no tight bend right at the plug.

About 10 minutes into Kingdom Come: Deliverance II at 4K, it showed 321W flowing through the connector. That figure only covers the 16-pin plug, since power the card draws from the PCIe slot never passes through the WireView. The bars on the front represent per-pin amperage readings, and I was seeing roughly 4.5A per pin, which checks out with the math. The hottest sensor, on the side that mates with the card, read 41 degrees Celsius. That's warm enough to notice with your fingers and nowhere near the 80°C default alarm. It can't tell me what my plug was doing before the WireView went in, but it suggests what I felt was ordinary. The temperature climbed to about 50 Celsius later, which still isn't concerning on its own. It also shows which power tier the cable is advertising through its sense pins. I'm running the triple 8-pin adapter that came with the card, and it signals 450W, which is what Nvidia specifies for the RTX 5080.

Now, if a reading stays over its limit for more than 10 seconds, the WireView will flag it on screen and sound an alarm. These limits are set to 10A per pin, 600W total, and 80 degrees on the connector. That alone doesn't save your system, but what does is an included Y-splitter that can tie into your motherboard's power switch, allowing it to shut the system down in the event of a high reading. What it doesn't do is load balance, which is an entirely different approach to protecting your GPU.

GPU power cables are still melting RTX 5090s, and Nvidia had the solution years ago

There's no end in sight for the 12V-2x6 standard

7
By  Ty Sherback

Why a GPU power plug needs a babysitter

12v-2x6 and 12VHPWR do not have a good reputation

The 12V-2x6 connector can carry up to 600W across six 12V pins, and the spec only requires each pin to handle 9.2A. At full load, that works out to a safety factor of roughly 1.1, compared with about 1.7 for the old 8-pin PCIe connector. There isn't much room for error here, and while it's true that on paper, everything checks out with the 5090, in reality, there are more variables at play.

One of the biggest variables is contact resistance. Every plug has some, but it varies from pin to pin, and it gets worse as contacts wear from being plugged and unplugged. Six wires in parallel split the current based on how much each path resists it, so when one contact degrades, its share gets pushed onto the others. The bad contact heats up on its own, and the pins picking up its slack heat up too, since heating rises with the square of the current. The connector's thin margin leaves little room to absorb that, and on cards that don't balance the load across the pins, nothing corrects for it.

Credit: TechPowerUp Forums (User: taka)

Nvidia has considered this before: the RTX 3090 Ti split its wires across three shunt resistors, so it could see and balance the load between groups. However, the Founders Edition RTX 4090 and 5090 treat all six as a single input, and these are the cards that spawned this entire product category in the first place. At 575W, a 5090 averages roughly 8A per pin even when everything is working as intended. My 5080 is a different story. Its 360W rating works out to about 5A per pin at most, and MSI doesn't advertise any per-pin sensing on the Shadow. For me, the WireView is a diagnostic tool and peace of mind, not a necessity.

The 12V-2x6 revision did fix one failure mode by shortening the sense pins, so a plug that isn't fully seated shouldn't deliver power. It doesn't help a fully seated plug with one degraded contact, and that's exactly what per-pin monitoring is for.

Why doesn’t Nvidia stick to 8-pin PCIe cables?

Nvidia's 12VHPWR woes still exist, making everyone think why not use 8-pin cables like before?

15
By  Tanveer Singh

Active load balancing is another approach

Adding real-time balancing to a card that doesn't have it

Credit: aquacomputer

The WireView Pro II simply takes the information it gets from the plug and acts upon it reactively, but there are other products that take a more proactive approach. Aqua Computer's Ampinel tries to do just that, sitting inline like the WireView but instead of just reacting to potentially hazardous readings, it uses series MOSFETs to raise the voltage drop on whichever line is overloaded, nudging current onto the others. It has a similar monitoring setup to the WireView, featuring an OLED screen with per-line current, an alarm system, and a shutdown path.

My crazy powerful gaming PC feels like a ticking time bomb

We shouldn't have to worry that high-end hardware will burn itself up.

8
By  Jacob Roach

Balancing still doesn't fix the core issue

The connector itself is the problem, and it's on Nvidia

Balancing doesn't add capacity, and it also doesn't fix the connector itself. The card decides how much total current it needs, so relieving one overloaded wire means shifting that current onto the others. That's definitely better than letting a single pin cook itself, but it's still a band-aid solution for a connector that's already short on headroom. A contact that's degrading will continue to do so while the balancer compensates for it.

Both of these approaches, reactive and proactive, are valid ways to keep your valuable card from cooking itself to death, and which one you ultimately choose to use on your card is probably better than nothing at all, though if you're like me and own a lower-wattage card, the chances of a failure are lower than if you're pushing the limits of Nvidia's flagship GPU.

WireView Pro II

The WireView Pro II is a device for measuring the power consumption of graphics cards. The 2nd Pro generation offers additional monitoring features in the form of per-pin power measurement, as well as an extended warranty and a TFT-IPS display.

$140 at Thermal Grizzly

item.title: Your ESP32 has a secret processor that keeps working while the rest of the chip is asleep
item.itunes:title: Your ESP32 has a secret processor that keeps working while the rest of the chip is asleep
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You might be familiar with the dual Xtensa cores on your ESP32, which divide the primary code and background activity among them. However, most people don't know about a separate coprocessor hiding on the same die. This Ultra-Low Power (ULP) coprocessor is a single core that stays awake even when the main CPU has gone to sleep. You only notice it when you need it, so it goes unnoticed in the majority of the projects.

However, it can keep your project alive for long periods of time. When you don't need the main CPU to perform heavy tasks regularly, the ULP becomes the star of the show, keeping things powered while sipping power.

This is why I keep buying ESP32 boards instead of more smart home gadgets

My home, my rules.

13
By  Samir Makwana

The ULP coprocessor is the part of the chip that never fully sleeps

It's not the core you want, but the one you need

The third core on your ESP32 is called "ULP" for a reason. Its whole purpose is to stay functional when nothing else on the board is awake. The main dual-core CPU and most of the memory shut down when your ESP32 goes into deep sleep. The ULP is exempt from this deep sleep because it runs on the board's Real-Time Clock (RTC) power domain, drawing minimal power.

As for memory access, it uses a small dedicated part of the RTC slow memory, typically 8KB on the classic ESP32, to store the program instructions and log data it needs to execute the simple tasks it's built for. For instance, the ESP32's main CPU consumes around 240 mA (or more) during active execution, whereas the ULP consumes around 200 µA, which is several orders of magnitude less. It even drops to as low as 10 µA in its deep sleep state.

Why the ESP32-S3 is the best $8 you'll ever spend on your smart home

Stop overpaying and ditch the cloud

By  Samir Makwana

It's tiny, but handles important functions while saving battery power

Without ULP, your battery-powered project wouldn't run for long

The ULP isn't a replacement for your main CPU cores. It's built to execute a narrow set of functions that isn't feasible for the main processor, at least if you want to conserve battery. Most sensor-based projects spend the overwhelming majority of their time doing nothing — checking a temperature that hasn't changed, a button that is still unpressed, or a water level that's stayed the same.

Executing these tasks on the main dual-core CPU is wasteful on a battery-powered project. The ULP is designated to monitor sensors, take ADC readings, poll GPIO pins, and check if a value has crossed a threshold. When your device needs to execute real tasks, such as connecting to Wi-Fi, processing data, or managing memory allocations, the ULP wakes up the main CPU.

The ULP optimizes battery life by taking over repetitive, low-stakes checking, while the power-intensive part of the chip only wakes up when it's really needed.

The ESP32 project I'm most proud of has no cloud, no app, and no gimmicks

Minimal build, maximum payoff.

2
By  Samir Makwana

Most people forget it exists until a project actually needs it

It can fly under the radar

When your ESP32 project doesn't need deep sleep optimization, it doesn't need to leverage the ULP coprocessor at all. Only when you need your device to run for months on a small battery will you build it around the ULP. A soil moisture sensor in your garden, a remote temperature sensor, or a leak detector under a sink can work for ages since the main chip stays fully off most of the time.

The ULP wakes up for periodic polling, saving most of the battery life. Using RTC memory, it stores the results which the main CPU needs to read once it wakes up. The ULP becomes apparent when people realize their chip had a coprocessor all along, waiting for a project that can make use of it. It has real hardware limitations, but that's by design. The ULP was never meant to perform more than basic, low-powered tasks, and it does that perfectly.

ESP32
Brand
AITRIP
Connectivity Features
UART, USB

The ESP32 is a fantastic development board that combines solid specs with an affordable price. Despite being cheaper than Arduino and Raspberry Pi Pico, it outperforms most of its rivals. Plus, the ESP32 even has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth functionality built into every board, making it great for projects where you can't physically keep the microcontroller connected to your PC at all times.

Pi-hole has its perks, but an ESP32 can handle DNS duties without a sweat

2
By  Ty Sherback

Your ESP32 is capable of running for far longer than you think

Unless your project needs always-on Wi-Fi or Bluetooth or perform frequent computations, you can use the ULP coprocessor to maximize its battery life. This additional core can run at miniscule levels of power and still keep your project alive. It allows your main chip to enter deep sleep while it works silently in the background.

item.title: I gave my 7-year-old laptop a second life with local AI, and it's surprisingly useful
item.itunes:title: I gave my 7-year-old laptop a second life with local AI, and it's surprisingly useful
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A seven-year-old laptop doesn't exactly sound like the kind of machine you'd pick for an AI experiment, especially since I've been enjoying using an RTX 4070 Ti-powered PC for a while now. Mine has long since been relegated to the occasional task, quietly sitting around while newer hardware does the heavy lifting. But I've always had a soft spot for old hardware, especially when there's still some life left in it.

Lately, I've been finding ways to make that life considerably more interesting. A handful of free local AI projects have turned this otherwise forgotten laptop into something I actually enjoy using again. Full disclosure — they haven't somehow "transformed" the laptop into a modern workstation, but they've certainly given me a reason to fire it up regularly again, which is more than I expected.

Trying to self-host LLMs made me realize local AI has a friction problem, not a quality problem

Think of it as the Linux desktop problem, all over again

30
By  Samarveer Singh

I turned my old laptop into a private PDF assistant

It can finally make sense of the documents I keep ignoring

It wasn't until I properly tried repurposing my old laptop into a PDF assistant that I realized exactly why it was such a tried and tested method. It also made sense for me, since the laptop, over years of collecting dust, had also accumulated a ridiculous collection of manuals, reference documents, articles, and assorted paperwork sitting on its multiple drives. I only open most of these when I desperately need one specific piece of information from a document I faintly recall. A small local model gives that forgotten machine an actual job.

I use Qwen3 4B at Q4_K_M for this process, which roughly takes up around 3GB on my laptop. With just 8GB total system RAM to spare and no useful dedicated VRAM, this model helps me stick to a relatively modest window of around 4–8K tokens.

The laptop I'm using is a 2019 Mi Notebook 14 with an Intel i5-10210U running at 1.60GHz, 8GB RAM, and 128 MB integrated VRAM.

Instead of uploading a PDF to a cloud chatbot, I can just point Qwen3 at it (it does require a vibe-coded Python script to turn all my PDFs into TXT files), and have it summarize or extract the info I actually need. Plus, when it comes to the longer, more technical documents, this feels considerably more useful than scrolling through 80 pages hoping the right keyword eventually reveals itself.

It's not the fastest process in the world, sure, but the important bit is that the documents stay on the machine. My PDFs contain personal information, work material, invoices, or anything else I'd rather not hand to an external AI service. The laptop isn't particularly fast at inference, but speed becomes a much smaller concern when the alternative is opening another browser tab and uploading everything.

I check these 4 numbers before downloading a local AI model, and tokens per second is dead last

Before your local AI runs, it needs to walk

1
By  Abhinav Raj

I let local AI clean up my digital mess

My old laptop became a surprisingly good file clerk

The next experiment was less glamorous, but more useful. I have accumulated years of files with names that tell me nothing. Screenshots, photos, PDFs, and random downloads have taken on all sorts of names — think IMG_4821, document-final-2, or Screenshot 2025-03-14. I wanted the laptop to fix that mess without uploading my files.

There's no reason Claude Code couldn't help me out with my local AI workflow, so I vibecoded a quick Python script that scans a folder, sends each image to Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, asks it for a short description, and uses that description to suggest a filename. Of course, I'm still the final authority, meaning nothing gets renamed until I approve the changes myself.

I deliberately kept an approval step between the model and my filesystem. Local AI is useful, but I don't trust a 3B model enough to let it rename hundreds of files unsupervised. My personal photos, screenshots, and documents never have to leave the laptop. The machine isn't particularly fast, but it can quietly organize my files in the background while keeping the data itself entirely under my control.

I replaced Claude with a local 9B model for a week, and it handled 95% of my work

Qwen 3.5 glides through the rest.

6
By  Anurag Singh

I had to ditch Ollama and go closer to the metal

llama.cpp makes my old laptop feel surprisingly capable

There's no denying that Ollama is a wonderfully convenient way to get local AI working on any piece of hardware, regardless of its age. I myself used Ollama for quite a while on my desktop PC before ditching it for Jan just recently. This old laptop, however, didn't have a lot of RAM for me to waste, and in the interest of squeezing out every last bit of performance from its seven-year-old processor, llama.cpp became the only way forward.

With llama.cpp, I work directly with GGUF models straight from Hugging Face. I even get control over things like context size, CPU threads, and GPU offloading. Of course, on an 8GB machine with Intel integrated graphics, CPU inference is pretty much the reality, but having that control when I need to exercise it (if ever) matters. A Qwen3 4B Q4_K_M model is small enough to remain practical without turning Windows into a slideshow.

Truth be told, the difference between Ollama and llama.cpp on my old laptop isn't magical, by any stretch of imagination. The latter gives me more control over my laptop, sure, but I still rest easy knowing that I'm making every MB of my total RAM count.

llama.cpp

Llama.cpp is an open-source framework that runs large language models locally on your computer. 

See at Official Website
I ran the same local LLM on an RTX 5070 laptop and one with an iGPU, and the difference was smaller than I expected

You don't need an expensive GPU to start running local AI.

10
By  Yash Patel

Maybe old hardware just needs a better reason to exist

Local AI has made the laptop interesting again.

A seven-year-old laptop isn't fast by any means, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise, either. There are moments when I can practically hear the Core i5-10210U negotiating with whatever I've asked it to do. But that has stopped mattering as much as I expected.

Local AI has made the laptop interesting again simply because this machine is now doing things I actually care about, and that's why it doesn't collect dust under my desk anymore. This second wind that the laptop has received is thanks to a new reason for using it, without any hardware upgrades involved.
